note: 1990 TECHNOLOGY: AUTHORED, NOT DERIVED. What this nation knew on 1 January 1990 is transcribed and sourced grant by grant, exactly like every other 1990 figure in this file, and is not read off tfp_trend - there was never a code path from the trend to the known set, and the zero that stood there was a claim about the world rather than an absence of one (BIBLE section 8 and iron rule 4, both amended 2026-08-30). THE PREDICATE IS SPLIT, and split by the technology's OWN EFFECT TYPE so that it is mechanically computable and never a per-nation judgement call. A node whose effects include MilitaryEfficiency, MilitaryStrength, DiffusionEmission or CostReduction is SOVEREIGNTY-SIDE: holding it means this nation could PRODUCE it, so operating an imported article does not qualify. Every other node is USE-SIDE: deployed and in operational use here is enough, whoever built it, because the effect such a node pays is a productivity, health or output effect and that effect is real in the country where the machine runs. Of the 48 technologies the tree lets anyone hold in 1990, 17 are sovereignty-side and 31 are use-side.

ALL 48 OF THE 1990-ELIGIBLE TECHNOLOGIES WERE RULED FOR THIS NATION, one at a time, against a standard published per technology rather than per country. 5 were held and are listed below with their citations; 43 were refused. The refused ids are named at the end of this note so that a reader can tell a cell that was examined and refused from a cell nobody looked at - those are different claims and the schema would otherwise flatten them into the same silence.

granted.source: NTPC's first gas-based combined-cycle stations - Anta (Rajasthan) and Auraiya (Uttar Pradesh) - were commissioned from 1989 on gas from the Hazira-Bijaipur-Jagdishpur pipeline, which was commissioned in 1987. FLAGGED: combined-cycle stations are normally commissioned gas-turbine-first with the steam bottoming cycle following a year or more later, so the risk in this cell is that on 1 January 1990 Anta was running open-cycle only. The station and the pipeline are checkable; the exact date the bottoming cycle was synchronised is not established here.

India's first digital E10B exchange was completed at Bombay (Worli-III) in 1983-84, with further E10B exchanges at Ahmedabad, Delhi, Madras and Calcutta; ITI's Mankapur factory manufactured the E10B under Alcatel-Thomson collaboration. India's first indigenously developed digital rural exchange, the 128-line C-DOT RAX, was installed at Kittur, Karnataka, on 22 July 1986.

APPLE (Ariane Passenger Payload Experiment), ISRO's first indigenous experimental geostationary communications satellite and India's first three-axis-stabilised geostationary spacecraft, was launched from Kourou on 19 June 1981 and used for television relay and radio networking experiments. Designed and built by ISRO in two years. WEAKEST OF THE NINE GRANTS: APPLE was experimental, and India's first ISRO-built operational INSAT (INSAT-2A) did not fly until July 1992 - the INSAT-1 series was built abroad.

Central Electronics Limited, Sahibabad, has manufactured crystalline silicon photovoltaic modules since 1977-78, and the Department of Non-Conventional Energy Sources, created in 1982, ran national programmes putting those modules into village street lighting, domestic lighting and irrigation pumping through the 1980s. India in 1990 was one of the largest rural photovoltaic markets in the world by number of installations, which is exactly what 'installed and generating at any material scale' asks for. This is a non-obvious grant and it is the one I would defend hardest against a reader who expects the 1990 board to be a wealth ordering.

Oral rehydration therapy was validated in the field in India: Dilip Mahalanabis and colleagues, working from the Johns Hopkins International Centre for Medical Research in Calcutta, treated cholera with oral rehydration salts in the Bangaon refugee camp in West Bengal in 1971 when intravenous fluids ran out, and case-fatality fell from roughly thirty per cent to a few per cent. That episode is the reason ORT became WHO policy. India then carried ORS through its national diarrhoeal disease control programme and the primary health centre network across the 1980s under the WHO/UNICEF child survival push, and the National Institute of Cholera and Enteric Diseases in Calcutta remained the reference institution.
